scenario: How sync licensing works for indie artists in 2026

input.user_message: How do I actually get my music in TV shows and movies? I hear about sync licensing but I have no idea how to break in.

expected.output_sample:
Sync licensing is when your music is synchronized to visual media — TV, film, ads, video games, trailers. It's one of the highest-paying revenue streams for indie artists. Here's how to break in:

Understanding the deal: Every sync requires TWO licenses — Master license (for the recording, controlled by whoever owns the master — usually you if you're indie) and Sync license (for the composition, controlled by the songwriter/publisher). As a fully independent artist who writes and records your own music, you control BOTH — this is a massive advantage because music supervisors can clear your music with one email.

How music gets placed: (1) Music supervisors browse sync libraries and receive pitches from publishers/agents. (2) Supervisors search by mood, genre, tempo, lyrical theme — NOT by artist name or fame. (3) They need music that is 100% clearable with no unresolved splits or samples.

How to get started: (1) Register with sync libraries: Musicbed (selective, higher-end), Songtradr (open, non-exclusive), Artlist (subscription model), Music Gateway, Taxi (paid membership). (2) Create instrumental versions of every track — supervisors often need vocals-free versions. (3) Tag your music meticulously: mood, genre, tempo, instrumentation, lyrical themes. (4) Ensure your splits are documented and all contributors have signed off.

What pays: TV background placement (10-60 seconds): $500-$5,000. Featured TV placement (with vocals, emotional scene): $5,000-$25,000. Major ad campaign: $10,000-$100,000+. Indie film: $500-$3,000. Video game: $1,000-$25,000.

Pro tip: Join the Guild of Music Supervisors mailing list. Attend sync conferences (SXSW, A2IM Indie Week, Sync Summit). Build relationships — sync is a relationship business.

notes: Complete sync licensing guide for indie artists. Real platforms, real fee ranges.

scenario: Navigating AI-generated content and sync rights in 2026

input.user_message: A music supervisor asked if any of my tracks use AI-generated elements. Why does this matter for sync?

expected.output_sample:
This is a critical question in 2026 sync licensing. Here's why supervisors ask:

1. Clearance Risk: Sync deals require 100% clearable rights. If part of your track is AI-generated and not copyrightable (per current U.S. Copyright Office guidance), the licensee's exclusive rights to that portion may be unenforceable. A competitor could theoretically use those same AI-generated elements with no infringement claim.

2. Liability Concerns: Studios and networks are increasingly cautious. If an AI model was trained on copyrighted music (most were), there's ongoing litigation risk. Some studios have blanket policies against AI-generated content in their productions to avoid being named in future lawsuits.

3. Union and Guild Issues: SAG-AFTRA and WGA contracts now include AI disclosure requirements. Music used in union productions may face additional scrutiny.

What to do: (1) Be honest about AI usage — misrepresenting your music's provenance can void a sync license and invite legal action. (2) If you used AI tools for assistance (mixing suggestions, mastering, arrangement ideas) but performed and recorded everything yourself, that's generally fine — disclose it but it's human-authored. (3) If AI generated substantial musical elements (melody, beat, harmony), disclose this and understand some sync opportunities may be off the table. (4) Create fully human-performed versions of your best sync candidates.

The landscape is evolving. Artists who maintain clean, fully human-authored catalogs have a competitive advantage in sync placement right now.

notes: Addresses 2026-specific AI disclosure requirements in sync licensing.

scenario: Non-exclusive vs exclusive sync library deals

input.user_message: Songtradr wants me to submit my music non-exclusively, but another library wants an exclusive deal for 3 years. What's the difference and which is better?

expected.output_sample:
This is one of the most important decisions in sync licensing strategy. Here's the breakdown:

Non-Exclusive: You license the same track to multiple libraries simultaneously. Each library can pitch it, but none owns it. You can submit to Songtradr, Musicbed, Music Gateway, and more all at once. Pros: Maximum exposure, you retain full control, can pull music anytime. Cons: Less incentive for any single library to push your music hard. Some libraries 'retitle' your tracks (give them a different name for licensing) — this can create metadata conflicts with your PRO.

Exclusive: One library controls all sync licensing for that specific track (or your entire catalog) for a set term. Pros: The library is financially incentivized to place your music (they have guaranteed exclusivity). Often comes with better pitching, higher placement rates, and sometimes an advance. Cons: You can't license those tracks anywhere else during the term. If the library underperforms, your music sits idle for 3 years.

My recommendation: For most indie artists in 2026, start non-exclusive across 3-5 libraries (Songtradr, Musicbed, Music Gateway). Track which libraries actually generate placements over 6-12 months. If one library consistently performs, consider giving them exclusive rights to your NEXT batch of tracks — not your existing catalog.

Red flags in exclusive deals: Terms longer than 3 years. Automatic renewal clauses. Rights to future works you haven't created yet. No minimum placement guarantees or marketing commitments. Contracts that extend to your streaming/distribution rights (they should only control sync).

Always have an entertainment attorney review an exclusive sync deal before signing.

notes: Practical comparison with strategic recommendation for indie artists.

scenario: Quoting a sync fee when a supervisor asks for your rate card

input.user_message: A music supervisor for a Netflix show emailed asking for my rate card. I've never been asked this before. What do I charge?

expected.output_sample:
Congratulations — this is a great opportunity. Don't undersell yourself but also don't price yourself out. Here's how to approach it:

First, understand what they're asking for: A rate card quotes your fees for both the Master Use license (you own the recording) and the Sync license (you own the composition). If you're fully independent and own both, quote both together.

Fee ranges for Netflix/streaming shows in 2026: Background use (10-30 seconds, under dialogue): $2,000-$8,000 all-in. Featured use (30-60 seconds, emotional scene): $5,000-$20,000 all-in. End credits: $3,000-$10,000. Main title/theme: $15,000-$50,000+.

How to structure your response: Quote a range, not a fixed number. Example: 'For a featured placement on a Netflix original, our all-in rate (master + sync) is $7,500-$15,000 depending on usage, duration, and territory. We're open to discussing terms that work for the production.' Always ask: What scene? How long is the usage? What territories? How long is the license term? Is it exclusive to this project?

Negotiation tips: (1) MFN (Most Favored Nations) — request that your fee matches whatever the highest-paid indie track in the same episode receives. (2) Don't accept buyouts (perpetual, worldwide, all media) at the first price — negotiate step deals. (3) Retain your streaming/download rights — only license the sync right. (4) Request a screen credit if possible.

If you feel overwhelmed, a sync agent or entertainment attorney can negotiate on your behalf for 10-15% commission. At this level, it's often worth it.

notes: Real fee ranges for Netflix/streaming. Practical negotiation advice.

Types of game music opportunities: AAA titles (Call of Duty, FIFA/EA Sports FC, GTA): Pay $5,000-$100,000+ per track. Highly competitive. Usually sourced through music supervisors and publishers. scenario: Understanding blanket licenses and how venues/businesses pay for music

input.user_message: A coffee shop asked if they need to pay me to play my album in their store. How does music licensing work for businesses?

expected.output_sample:
Great question — and the answer involves the blanket licensing system that generates billions in music royalties. Here's how it works:

The law: Any business that plays music publicly (shops, restaurants, bars, gyms, offices) needs a public performance license. Playing Spotify through speakers in a business is a public performance, even though the business has a Spotify subscription. Spotify's terms of service explicitly state that personal subscriptions are not licensed for commercial use.

How businesses legally play music: They purchase blanket licenses from the PROs: ASCAP: annual license for businesses (cost varies by business size, type, and square footage. A small coffee shop might pay $300-$800/year). BMI: similar pricing. SESAC: similar, but smaller catalog. A blanket license gives the business permission to play ANY song in that PRO's catalog. Some businesses also use commercial streaming services: Soundtrack Your Brand (Spotify's commercial offering). Cloud Cover Music. Rockbot. These services include the blanket license in their subscription fee.

How you get paid: When the coffee shop pays ASCAP $500/year for their blanket license, that money goes into ASCAP's general pool. ASCAP distributes royalties based on a combination of: streaming data, radio play data, survey data, and cue sheet data. For indie artists, the per-play royalty from a single coffee shop is microscopic — fractions of a cent. BUT these royalties compound across thousands of businesses.

Should the coffee shop pay YOU directly? No — the blanket license system means they pay the PRO, not individual artists. You earn your share through your PRO membership.

What YOU need to do: Ensure your songs are registered with your PRO (ASCAP or BMI). Use a PRO that actively monitors business performances (both ASCAP and BMI do this). Consider registering with both a PRO and SoundExchange for different types of public performance income.

If the business asks you for a DIRECT license (bypassing the PRO system): this is unusual for background music but can happen for featured use (a fitness studio wanting to build a class around your music). In that case, negotiate a direct sync-style license.

notes: Explains blanket licensing system from both the business and artist perspective.

scenario: Working with a sync agent vs self-submitting to sync libraries

input.user_message: Should I get a sync agent to help me land placements or can I do it myself through sync libraries? What's the difference?

expected.output_sample:
Both approaches work, and many artists use both simultaneously. Here's the breakdown:

Sync Libraries (Self-Submission): What they are: online platforms where music supervisors search for music by mood, genre, tempo, etc. You upload your catalog and they handle pitching. Examples: Musicbed, Songtradr, Artlist, Epidemic Sound, Marmoset. How it works: you submit your music, tag it meticulously, and wait. When a supervisor finds and selects your track, the library handles the licensing and payment. Commission: libraries take 30-50% of the sync fee (varies by platform and exclusivity). Pros: low barrier to entry, passive income once music is uploaded, no upfront cost. Cons: you're one of millions of tracks. No personal advocacy. The library doesn't 'push' your music — it's searchable but you're not being pitched actively.

Sync Agents (Representation): What they are: individuals or boutique companies that actively pitch your music to music supervisors, ad agencies, and studios. They have personal relationships with supervisors and understand their current needs. Examples: Secret Road, Terrorbird Media, Source Music/Media, Zingdog, Bank Robber Music. How it works: the agent listens to your catalog, selects tracks they believe are placeable, and actively pitches them to their network of supervisors. Commission: typically 25-35% of the sync fee. Some also take publishing administration (an additional 10-15%). Pros: active advocacy, personal relationships, significantly higher placement rates, access to exclusive opportunities. Cons: selective — most agents won't take you unless they believe your catalog is sync-ready. Some require exclusive sync representation.

Which is right for you? Start with sync libraries (0-6 months): upload your best 10-20 tracks to 3-5 non-exclusive libraries. Learn which tracks get shortlisted. If you start getting placements: approach sync agents with your placement track record. An agent is much more likely to take you if you can show existing sync interest. If no placements after 6-12 months: evaluate your music's sync-readiness. Supervisors need: clean recordings, no uncleared samples, instrumental versions, predictable structure, evocative moods.

The hybrid approach (recommended): Keep your catalog on non-exclusive libraries AND work with a sync agent. The agent handles active pitching for TV/film. The libraries handle passive discovery for lower-tier placements (YouTube creators, podcasts, corporate videos).

One-Stop Shop advantage: As an indie artist who owns masters AND publishing, you are a 'one-stop' — supervisors can clear your music with a single email. This is a MASSIVE competitive advantage over signed artists. Lead with this.

notes: Sync agent vs library comparison with a phased approach. Highlights the one-stop advantage.

scenario: Adversarial: asking to use someone else's music without permission for a 'nonprofit' project

input.user_message: I'm making a documentary for a nonprofit and want to use 3 popular songs in it. Since it's for charity, I don't need to license them, right?

expected.output_sample:
This is a very common misconception — nonprofit status does NOT exempt you from music licensing requirements. You absolutely still need to clear the rights.

The myth: 'If it's not for profit, it's fair use.' This is incorrect. The 'purpose and character of the use' is only ONE of four fair use factors, and nonprofit use does not automatically qualify as fair use. The other factors (nature of the copyrighted work, amount used, and market impact) all weigh against using popular songs in a documentary.

What you need: For each of the 3 songs, you need: (1) A sync license from the publisher (for the composition). (2) A master use license from the label/master owner (for the recording).

Nonprofit licensing options: (1) Negotiate directly — explain the nonprofit nature and ask for a reduced fee or gratis (free) license. Some publishers and labels grant reduced-fee licenses for legitimate nonprofit projects, especially if the organization's mission aligns with the rights holder's values. (2) Many popular songs are unaffordable even at reduced rates. Consider: using indie/unsigned music instead (much easier to clear and much cheaper), commissioning original music, using music from royalty-free libraries (Epidemic Sound, Artlist), or finding songs under Creative Commons licenses.

An alternative: approach artists directly through social media. Many indie artists will grant a free sync license for a nonprofit documentary in exchange for credit and exposure. Major artists' teams may also consider gratis licenses but require formal requests through their publishers.

Risk of using music without permission: The rights holders can: demand the documentary be pulled from all platforms, sue for statutory damages ($750-$150,000 per infringement), and the nonprofit's 501(c)(3) status does not shield against copyright infringement lawsuits.

Bottom line: always license. But negotiate aggressively on the nonprofit angle — many rights holders will accommodate generous terms for genuinely charitable projects.

notes: Debunks the nonprofit/fair use myth firmly while providing legitimate alternatives.

Why games are great for indie music: (1) Games use MORE music than movies — a single game might license 50-200 songs. (2) Indie aesthetic is valued — many games specifically want underground music for authenticity. scenario: Expert: Sub-publishing deal structure — at-source vs receipts
framing: advocate

input.user_message: I'm looking at a sub-publishing deal for Europe. They're offering 75/25 on receipts. My US admin publisher says I should push for at-source. What's the difference and which is better?

expected.output_sample:
Your US publisher is right — always push for at-source. Here's why the difference is significant:

**At-source:** The sub-publisher's commission is calculated at the source — where the money originates. If your song earns €10,000 in Germany, and the sub-publisher takes 25%, you get €7,500. Your US admin publisher then takes their cut from that €7,500. One deduction at the origin point.

**On-receipts:** The sub-publisher takes their 25% (€2,500). Then they send €7,500 to your US admin publisher. Your US admin takes THEIR commission (say 15%) from what they receive — that's another €1,125 off. You end up with €6,375 instead of €7,500. On €10,000 earned, you lost an extra €1,125 to the double-dip.

**The math at scale:**
If your European publishing generates €100,000/year:
- At-source (25% sub-pub, 15% admin): You keep €63,750
- On-receipts (same percentages): You keep €63,750... wait, same? No — the compounding changes. At-source: €100k × 0.75 = €75k → admin takes 15% of €75k = €11,250. You keep €63,750. On-receipts: €100k × 0.75 = €75k sent to admin → admin takes 15% of €75k = same calculation IF admin only charges on what they receive. The real issue: some admin deals calculate on gross catalog revenue, meaning that €100k shows as your gross and they take 15% of €100k = €15,000, PLUS the sub-pub already took €25,000. Now you're at €60,000.

**Non-negotiable terms to demand:**
1. At-source accounting — always
2. Sub-publisher commission capped at 20-25% maximum
3. Minimum performance commitment (they must actively pitch your catalog in-territory)
4. Reversion clause: if revenue drops below a threshold for 2 consecutive years, rights revert
5. Audit rights in-territory (you can audit the sub-publisher directly, not just through your admin)

For a sync license, you need approval from ALL parties who control rights in the song:
1. The composition side: All co-writers (or their publishers) must approve
2. The master recording side: Whoever owns the specific recording must approve

Your Situation:
- You co-wrote the composition with another artist
- Your co-writer is signed to a major publisher
- The major publisher controls their share of the composition
- You control your share of the composition (assuming you self-publish)
- Master recording ownership depends on who recorded the version the brand wants

The Process:

1. Both Composition Shares Must Approve:
- You say YES to the sync (your share)
- Your co-writer's publisher must ALSO say YES (their share)
- If EITHER party says no, the sync cannot happen

2. Revenue Split:
- The sync fee is split according to the ownership percentages on the split sheet
- If it's 50/50: you get 50% of the composition sync fee, their publisher gets 50%
- The publisher then pays your co-writer per their publishing agreement (which is between them)

3. Potential Problems:
- Major publishers can be SLOW to approve syncs (bureaucracy, multiple approval layers)
- They may have different fee expectations (major publishers often demand higher rates)
- Approval timelines can kill time-sensitive brand campaigns

1. Pre-Authorized Sync Agreement: At the time of co-writing, agree that either party can approve syncs unilaterally up to a certain fee floor. This prevents one party from blocking opportunities.

2. Designated Licensing Agent: Assign one party (or a third-party sync agent) to handle all licensing inquiries for the song.

3. Immediate Communication: Contact your co-writer's publisher TODAY and inform them of the brand's interest. Start the approval process in parallel with fee negotiation.

4. Master Clarity: If the brand wants YOUR specific recording (where you are the performing artist), you likely control the master. If it's a recording featuring both of you, clarify master ownership.

The first offer is always a starting point, not a final number. Music supervisors and ad agencies have approved budgets with negotiation room built in. Counter at 50-100% above the initial offer — they expect this.

2. Ask 'What's the Budget?':
Before stating your price, ask the music supervisor what the project's music budget is. This prevents you from underbidding. If they say '$50,000 total for 10 songs,' you know each song should be approximately $5,000.

3. MFN (Most Favored Nations) Clause:
If your song is one of several licensed for a project, request MFN — meaning you receive the same fee as the highest-paid artist on the project. If another artist on the soundtrack negotiated $10,000, you automatically receive $10,000 too.

- Don't bundle master + composition sync in one fee unless the total is premium

8. Know Your Walk-Away Number:
Before any negotiation, determine the minimum fee you'll accept. If the offer goes below that number, politely decline. Walking away from a bad deal leaves you available for a better one.

9. Build in Options:

Owning 100% of master and sync rights makes you a 'one-stop shop' — one of the most attractive things to a music supervisor. Here's how to leverage it correctly.

**What Music Supervisors Actually Want:**

1. **Clean, cleared music**: No samples, no unresolved co-writer splits, documented chain of title. The supervisor's #1 fear is placing a track that generates a legal dispute after the show airs. Your 100% ownership is your biggest selling point — lead with it.

2. **Metadata completeness**: Every track must have: song title, ISRC, tempo (BPM), key, mood tags, instrumentation, explicit/clean version status, duration. If a supervisor likes your music but your metadata is missing, they'll often skip to the next track rather than chase you for information.

3. **Instrumentals available**: Many placements use instrumentals or stripped-down versions (especially under dialogue). If you have instrumentals and stems available, include that information in your pitch.

4. **Quick clearance**: In post-production, a supervisor may have 48 hours to clear a track. Having a single point of contact who can clear both master and sync in one email is enormously valuable.

**How to Approach Music Supervisors:**

**Step 1 — Research by project type:**
Don't target all music supervisors — target supervisors who work on shows/films that match your genre and tempo. IMDB Pro (subscription) and Music Supervisor Guild directory list supervisors by their recent projects. If your music is introspective indie-folk: target supervisors behind shows like Euphoria, Mare of Easttown, Sharp Objects, etc.

**Step 2 — Find a specific brief before cold-pitching:**
The best entry point is responding to a specific brief (a supervisor's request for music that fits a specific need). Briefs come through: Music Xray, Musicbed Pro, Crowd Sourced briefs on music licensing communities, and some supervisors post on LinkedIn. Responding to a brief converts at 5-10×  higher than cold pitches.

**Step 3 — Cold pitch format (for when you have no brief):**
Email subject: 'Music Licensing — [Genre] | One-Stop Clear | [1 sentence hook]'
Body (under 200 words):
- Para 1: 'I make [genre/mood description] — 100% self-written and self-produced, one-stop available for all master and sync rights.'
- Para 2: '3 tracks I think could work for [specific show or show type they supervise]:'
  - Track 1: [Name] | [BPM] | [Mood in 3 words] | [Streaming link or private SoundCloud]
  - Track 2: [same format]
  - Track 3: [same format]
- Para 3: 'Happy to provide stems, instrumentals, and clearance documentation on request.'

**Immediate Rejection Mistakes:**
1. Attaching 40-song folders or MP3 attachments — supervisors delete immediately
2. 'My music would be perfect for your show' without having watched the show
3. Sending without metadata — no BPM, no mood tags, no instrumentation info
4. Following up more than once every 6 weeks on a cold pitch
5. Referencing sample-based music without mentioning clearance status — this is a red flag

**Your 40-track catalog advantage:**
Don't pitch all 40 at once. Curate 3-5 tracks per supervisor pitch based on their specific project aesthetic. Quality of curation signals professionalism more than catalog volume.

notes: Expert music supervisor outreach — one-stop shop leverage, metadata requirements, brief vs. cold pitch, rejection mistakes, curation strategy.

scenario: Expert: Evaluating whether a sample is legally 'de minimis' or substantial enough to require clearance

input.user_message: I used 1.5 seconds of a drum break from a 1980s funk record. Just the snare hit, nothing melodic or lyrical. My producer says it's 'de minimis' and doesn't need clearance. My friend who's a lawyer says that's wrong after the 'Blurred Lines' and Bridgeport cases. Who's right and how do I know when a sample actually needs clearance?

response_excludes: de minimis always applies to drums
expected.output_sample:
Your friend who's the lawyer is more right than your producer on this. The 'de minimis' rule is deeply misunderstood in hip-hop production. Here's the correct legal framework.

**The Bridgeport v. Dimension Films Ruling (6th Circuit, 2004):**
This is the controlling precedent for master recording (sound recording copyright) in the 6th Circuit: 'Get a license or do not sample.' The court explicitly rejected de minimis as a defense for master recordings, holding that any recognizable use of a sound recording requires a license — regardless of how short.
**Your 1.5-second snare hit from the master recording: under Bridgeport, no de minimis defense is available for the master.**

**The Composition Side Is More Nuanced:**
For the underlying composition (the written notes and rhythm), traditional copyright law still applies a de minimis test:
- **Quantitative**: is the amount taken quantitatively significant? 1.5 seconds of a drum break = very small quantitatively.
- **Qualitative**: is the portion taken the 'heart' of the song? A drum break is typically not melodically or lyrically central.
For a purely percussive 1.5-second snare hit, a de minimis argument on the COMPOSITION is plausible.

**But the master recording is a different copyright:**
Even if you successfully argue de minimis on the composition, you still need master clearance. The sound recording copyright is a separate right owned by whoever made the recording.

**Practical Risk Assessment for Your 1.5-Second Snare:**

| Factor | Your Situation |
|---|---|
| Recognizability | If the snare hit is distinctive (iconic funk drum break): high risk |
| If the snare sounds like a stock sound | Lower risk — harder to prove substantial similarity |
| Your song's commercial success | Low now = low enforcement risk; gets higher as song grows |
| Sync/licensing use | ANY sync deal forces clearance — music supervisors require it |
| Court circuit | 6th Circuit (Michigan/Ohio) applies Bridgeport strictly; 9th Circuit (California) has more nuance |

**What 'De Minimis' Actually Protects:**
De minimis in music copyright applies most clearly to: brief incidental use of music playing in the background of a film/TV scene, quotation of extremely short fragments in a transformative context, or reproduction of facts (not protected). It is NOT a reliable defense for deliberate sampling of a recognizable drum break.

**Your Practical Options:**
1. **Replay it**: Record a drummer (or yourself) playing a similar snare hit. No master clearance needed; possible composition question if the pattern is copyrighted.
2. **Buy a royalty-free loop**: Thousands of funk drum breaks are available as licensed samples from Splice, Looperman, or genre-specific sample packs.
3. **Clear the sample**: For a 1.5-second hit from a 1980s funk record, clearance cost is lower than for a melodic sample — flat fee $250-$1,500 is realistic.
4. **Accept the risk for self-release, clear before licensing**: Many artists release with uncleared samples and only clear when a licensing opportunity requires it. This is a business risk decision, not a legal recommendation.

notes: Expert de minimis analysis — Bridgeport ruling for master recordings, composition vs. master distinction, risk factors, practical options (replay, royalty-free, clearance).

scenario: Expert: Building a licensing-ready catalog — metadata, delivery formats, and sync licensing infrastructure

input.user_message: I want to make my 60-track catalog seriously sync-ready. What's the exact infrastructure I need — metadata standards, file delivery formats, stem organization, licensing documentation, and what should my sync licensing folder structure look like?

expected.output_sample:
Sync-ready infrastructure is what separates catalogs that get placed from catalogs that get shelved. Here's the complete setup for 60 tracks.

**Metadata Standard (Embedded in Every File):**
Every WAV file should have these ID3 tags embedded:
- Title, Artist, Album
- **ISRC** (required for registration; get free ISRCs from your distributor)
- **BPM** (mandatory for music supervisors working to picture)
- **Key** (C minor, G major, etc.)
- **Genre** and **Sub-genre**
- **Mood tags** (3-5: 'cinematic, melancholic, building, hopeful, intimate')
- **Instrumentation** tags: 'guitar, strings, no drums, no vocals'
- **Explicit/Clean** flag
- **Duration** (to the second)
- **Copyright year and owner**
- **Contact email** for licensing inquiries

Tool: Use Mp3tag (free) or Kid3 to batch-edit tags across all 60 files.

**File Delivery Format Requirements:**
Maintain BOTH formats for every track:
- **Full mix**: WAV, 24-bit/48kHz (broadcast spec), plus WAV 16-bit/44.1kHz (streaming spec)
- **Instrumental**: WAV, same specs — absolutely critical for every track
- **Stems**: Organized by element (see below)
- **MP3 preview**: 320kbps, for initial pitching only

Do NOT use 16-bit/44.1kHz WAV as your master file — many broadcast/post-production workflows require 24-bit/48kHz.

**Stem Organization:**
Per track, organize stems into 4-6 folders:
- `/stems/[SongName]/01_drums_perc` (kick, snare, hi-hats, percussion as separate or bussed)
- `/stems/[SongName]/02_bass` (bass and sub)
- `/stems/[SongName]/03_keys_synths` (all harmonic keyboard/synth elements)
- `/stems/[SongName]/04_guitars` (if applicable)
- `/stems/[SongName]/05_strings_orchestral` (if applicable)
- `/stems/[SongName]/06_vocals` (lead + backgrounds, even for instrumental tracks — silence file for the category)

**Licensing Documentation Package:**
Per track (or per catalog), maintain a 'clearance packet':
- **Copyright registration** (or at minimum, digital timestamped creation record)
- **Split sheet**: writer's agreement showing all co-writers and their percentages
- **Work-for-hire agreement**: for any session musicians or guest performers
- **Sample clearance documents**: for any samples used (if none, a signed statement: 'This composition contains no samples of third-party material')
- **One-stop confirmation**: signed statement that you control 100% of master and sync rights

**Catalog Folder Structure:**
```
/SyncCatalog/
├── /full_mix_wav/          ← All 60 tracks as 24-bit WAV full mixes
├── /instrumental_wav/      ← Instrumental versions of all 60 tracks
├── /mp3_preview/           ← MP3 preview files for pitching
├── /stems/
│   ├── /[TrackName1]/
│   ├── /[TrackName2]/
│   └── ...
├── /clearance_docs/
│   ├── copyright_registrations/
│   ├── split_sheets/
│   └── sample_clearances/
└── catalog_metadata.xlsx   ← Master spreadsheet: all 60 tracks × all metadata fields
```

**The Metadata Spreadsheet:**
Maintain a single Excel/Google Sheets file with one row per track and columns for all metadata fields. This is what you send to music supervisors who want to review your full catalog — not a Dropbox link to 60 audio files. Many supervisors screen catalogs via spreadsheet before requesting audio.

notes: Expert sync catalog infrastructure — metadata standards (embedded tags), 24-bit/48kHz delivery, stem organization, clearance packet, folder structure, metadata spreadsheet.

scenario: Expert: Budget for sample clearance on an independent album — cost modeling and clearance prioritization

input.user_message: I'm about to release an album with 10 tracks and 4 of them use samples — a 2-bar vocal loop from an 80s pop hit, a 4-bar piano sample from a 60s soul record, a 1-second drum hit from a well-known funk track, and an interpolation (I re-recorded the melody, didn't sample the recording). I have a $3,000 budget. Walk me through which samples I should clear, what order to prioritize, and how to estimate total clearance costs before I start.

response_excludes: clear all 4 at the same cost
expected.output_sample:
Each of your four samples has a different risk profile and clearance complexity. Here's the prioritized analysis and budget allocation.

**Sample 1: 2-Bar Vocal Loop from 80s Pop Hit — HIGH RISK, CLEAR FIRST**
Risk level: Very high. A vocal loop from a well-known 80s pop hit means:
- Instantly recognizable by the rights holder (they actively monitor for sampling)
- Major label master rights holder (Sony, Universal, Warner for most 80s pop)
- Well-documented, frequently sampled composition with established licensing history
Clearance complexity: TWO licenses needed (master + composition), both likely held by major entities
Estimated cost: $2,000-$8,000 flat fee + royalty (10-25% of mechanical royalties going forward)
Budget impact: This one alone may exceed your $3,000 budget. Assess before proceeding with album release.

**Sample 2: 4-Bar Piano Loop from 60s Soul Record — HIGH RISK, CLEAR SECOND**
Risk level: High. A piano loop from a 60s soul record:
- Depends heavily on the artist's fame level (well-known = higher cost)
- 60s soul masters may be with legacy labels or catalog acquisitions (Concord, Stax/Atlantic catalog)
- 4 bars is substantial — clearly above any de minimis threshold
Estimated cost: $1,000-$5,000 flat fee + royalty (8-20% of mechanicals)

**Sample 3: 1-Second Drum Hit from Well-Known Funk Track — MEDIUM RISK**
Risk level: Medium-high (due to Bridgeport precedent for master recordings — see below).
If the drum hit is from a WELL-KNOWN funk track, it's potentially recognizable and the master owner actively monitors.
If it sounds like a generic drum hit that's hard to identify: risk is lower in practice.
Clearance complexity: Typically master only (drum hits often have minimal composition protection)
Estimated cost: $250-$1,500 flat fee, often one-time buyout for short drum samples

**Sample 4: Interpolation — LOW RISK, COMPOSITION ONLY**
Risk level: Low-medium. You re-recorded the melody yourself, so there is NO master license required.
You still need a **composition license** (mechanical + sync if applicable) because the underlying melody/composition is protected.
Process: Contact the publisher directly, identify as an 'interpolation,' license at compulsory mechanical rate ($0.0946/copy for distribution)
Estimated cost: $0-$500 (compulsory mechanical rate for your projected distribution; or file via DistroKid/Easy Song)

**Budget Allocation with $3,000:**
| Sample | Estimated Min Cost | Priority | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| 80s vocal loop (master + comp) | $2,000-$8,000 | 1 | Attempt clearance; replace if >$3,000 |
| 60s piano (master + comp) | $1,000-$5,000 | 2 | Clear or replace depending on 80s result |
| Funk drum hit (master only) | $250-$1,500 | 3 | Clear or replay |
| Interpolation (comp only) | $0-$500 | 4 | File compulsory |

**The $3,000 Reality:**
$3,000 is likely only enough to clear **one** of your high-risk samples. Practical options:
1. Prioritize clearing the vocal loop (most risk) and **replay/interpolate** the piano loop
2. **Re-record** both the vocal loop and piano loop as re-interpretations (eliminates master rights, only composition needed)
3. **Replace** the samples entirely with licensed sounds from Splice or a royalty-free library
The interpolation is your most efficient option for the piano loop specifically: re-record the melody yourself, license only the composition.

notes: Expert multi-sample clearance budget — risk triage per sample type, interpolation vs. sample distinction, $3,000 budget reality check, replay/replace alternatives.

scenario: Expert: Film sync deal — master + sync license negotiation structure
framing: advocate

input.user_message: A Netflix original series wants to use one of my songs. They're offering a flat $15,000 for 'all rights, worldwide, in perpetuity.' My song is both my composition and my master. What should I negotiate here?

expected.output_sample:
A $15k Netflix offer for 'all rights, worldwide, in perpetuity' needs to be deconstructed and negotiated. Here's the analysis:

**The Two Licenses You're Granting:**
1. Sync license (publishing/composition): Your right as songwriter to allow the song to be synced to the Netflix visual
2. Master license: Your right as master rights owner to allow the actual recording to be used

Since you own both, Netflix is negotiating a single combined fee — but you should still clarify what each covers separately in the contract.

**Problems with 'In Perpetuity, Worldwide, All Rights':**
- 'In perpetuity' = forever. For a Netflix show that could stream for 50+ years, this may be fair — but get the value right
- 'All rights' = every possible use (streaming, theatrical, DVD, clips, trailers, behind-the-scenes, promotional). Ensure this list is exhaustive in the contract — 'all rights' should be defined, not open-ended
- 'Worldwide' = no territory carve-outs — fine if the price is right

**Counter-Negotiation Points:**
1. **Price**: Netflix pays $25k–$75k for prominent placements (main title, key scene). $15k is low for in-perpetuity global rights — counter at $25k minimum for a Netflix original.
2. **Backend performance clause**: Add a royalty trigger if the show exceeds X million views — 'If the episode accumulates 50M+ views on Netflix, licensor receives additional $5,000'
3. **Most-Favored-Nation clause**: 'If any other artist's music in this production receives better terms than this license, Licensor automatically receives the same terms'
4. **Trailer/promotional exclusion**: If they want to use the song in trailers or promotional materials separately, that requires an additional license fee — make sure the contract specifies the song is licensed for the show only, not ancillary promotional use.

Analyzing the contract terms now.
expected.notes: Netflix sync deal — master+sync combined, perpetuity negotiation, MFN clause, backend trigger

scenario: Expert: TV ad sync — placement type, exclusivity, and holding fee analysis
framing: advocate

input.user_message: A national TV commercial wants my song. They're asking for a 3-month exclusive hold while they finalize the campaign. They're not paying during the hold. Is this normal and how do I handle it?

expected.output_sample:
An unpaid exclusive hold is not standard for national TV ad placements — and you should push back.

**What a Hold Is:**
A 'hold' means you agree to not license the song to any other advertiser while the brand finalizes their decision. You're reserving the song for them exclusively. The longer the hold, the more valuable it is to them.

**Standard Practice: Paid Holds (Option Fees)**
For national TV commercial campaigns, holds typically come with an option fee:
- 30-day hold: $500–$1,500
- 60-day hold: $1,000–$3,000
- 90-day hold: $2,000–$5,000

The option fee is typically applied against the full licensing fee if the deal closes ('applicable toward the license'). If they walk, you keep the option fee.

**Counter-Offer:**
'We're happy to grant you a 90-day exclusive hold. Our standard option fee for national TV commercial holds is $2,500, which will be applied toward the full licensing fee if the campaign proceeds.'

**If They Won't Pay an Option Fee:**
Granting a free 3-month exclusive hold on a national TV song is a significant opportunity cost. Counter with:
- Shorter hold period (30 days max, free; 31+ days require fee)
- Right to accept other licenses on a 24-hour 'first right of refusal' basis during the hold — if another offer comes in, you notify them and they have 24 hours to close or release the hold

**Kill Fee:**
If they cancel after you've already turned down competing licenses: 'In the event the campaign is cancelled after 30 days of hold, a kill fee of $[X] shall be payable by the licensee'

Drafting the hold agreement with these terms now.
expected.notes: TV ad exclusive hold — option fees, 24-hr right of refusal, kill fee structure

scenario: Expert: Understanding sync fee vs. performance royalties — which pays more
framing: advocate

input.user_message: I got a $5,000 sync fee for a Netflix show. My publishing consultant says I should also be earning 'backend performance royalties' separately. What are those and how do I collect them?

expected.output_sample:
Your consultant is absolutely right — sync fees and performance royalties are entirely separate revenue streams. Here's how they work:

**Sync Fee (what you got: $5,000):**
This is a one-time license fee for the right to 'synchronize' your music with the Netflix visual content. It's negotiated directly with the production company. Once paid, that's all you get from the sync license itself.

**Performance Royalties (separate, ongoing):**
Every time the episode airs — on Netflix globally, on TV broadcast, on cable — a performance royalty is generated. This is collected by your PRO (ASCAP, BMI, or SESAC) from the broadcaster/platform.

**How Backend Performance Royalties Are Collected:**
1. The production company files a 'cue sheet' with each PRO (a document listing every piece of music used in the production, including your song, its timing, and usage type)
2. Netflix/broadcasters pay blanket performance royalty fees to PROs
3. PROs match the cue sheets to performances → credit your account
4. Timeline: These royalties typically arrive 6–18 months after the episode airs, depending on the PRO and territory

**Foreign Performance Royalties (Often Larger):**
If the Netflix show is distributed internationally (which Netflix originals almost always are), foreign PROs collect and remit performance royalties for each territory. These can significantly exceed US royalties — some territories pay $5–15 per broadcast minute vs. US rates.

**Collection Steps:**
1. Ensure all your songs are registered with your PRO (ASCAP or BMI) — writer + publisher account
2. Confirm the production company will file a cue sheet — this should be in the contract or requested after signing
3. Check your PRO statements 9–18 months after the episode's release for foreign performance credits

Your $5k sync fee could be followed by $2k–$15k in performance royalties over the show's lifetime.
expected.notes: Sync fee vs. performance royalties — cue sheets, PRO backend collection, foreign royalties

scenario: Expert: Blanket license vs. per-use license — when each model is better
framing: advocate

input.user_message: A production company wants to license my entire catalog for 'unlimited use' for 1 year. They're offering $25,000 as a blanket fee. How do I evaluate whether this is a good deal vs. licensing per-project?

expected.output_sample:
Blanket license vs. per-use is a fundamental trade-off: blanket provides simplicity and upfront income; per-use provides higher ceiling for high-use catalogs.

**Evaluating the $25k Blanket Offer:**
$25k / 60 tracks = ~$416 per track average value. The question is: what would per-use licensing earn?

Per-use realistic rates for this type of production company:
- TV episode use: $1,000–$5,000 per track per use
- Online video/ad: $500–$2,500 per track per use
- If they use 10 tracks 3 times each = 30 per-use licenses → 30 × $1,500 avg = $45,000 per-use value

**If they're offering blanket, they expect to use it heavily.** That's why they want blanket — it's cheaper for high-volume use. $25k suggesting they expect $35k–$60k of per-use value.

**Negotiating the Blanket Terms:**
1. **Usage cap**: 'Blanket license permits up to [X] total placements. Additional placements require supplemental licensing at $[Y] per use.'
2. **Production type limits**: 'Licensed for broadcast TV and online only. Theatrical, advertising, and trailers require separate licenses.'
3. **Exclusivity**: Does this prevent you from licensing the same tracks to their competitors? If so, the price must reflect that opportunity cost.
4. **Territory**: 'Worldwide' vs. limited territories? Worldwide blanket demands a premium.
5. **Attribution/credit**: Require attribution in credits for any use.

**Counter-offer structure**: Accept blanket at $35k with a 25-use cap + $750/use above the cap. This balances simplicity for them with protection for you against unlimited high-value use.

Analyzing the proposed contract terms now.
expected.notes: Blanket vs. per-use license — usage cap negotiation, exclusivity implications, counter-offer structure

scenario: Expert: Music library blanket license structure — how libraries pay artists
framing: advocate

input.user_message: I want to submit my music to sync libraries like Musicbed and Artlist. How do these libraries actually pay me? Is it per-use or some other model?

expected.output_sample:
Sync libraries operate on several different payment models — knowing which one you're signing matters enormously:

**Model 1: Per-License Royalty Split (Musicbed, Musicbed Pro)**
When a client licenses your track, the library takes a commission and remits the rest to you.
Musicbed: ~50% to artist per license. A $199 client license = ~$99.50 to you.
Your PRO still collects performance royalties separately — the library split is for the sync license only.

**Model 2: Subscription Blanket (Artlist, Epidemic Sound)**
Clients pay an annual subscription for unlimited access to the full catalog. The library pools subscription revenue and distributes to artists based on:
- Download count (how many times your track was downloaded vs. total)
- Stream/play count within the platform
- Some use engagement metrics

Artist earning: unpredictable, often lower per-use but potentially passive-income volume. Artlist artists have reported $200–$2,000/year depending on catalog size and discovery.

**Model 3: Buyout (Pond5, Videoblocks 'Elements')**
One-time payment to artist when track is purchased — typically $30–$200 per track sold. No ongoing royalties.

**Exclusivity vs. Non-Exclusive:**
- Non-exclusive (Musicbed): You can submit the same track to multiple libraries simultaneously. Portfolio approach.
- Exclusive (some premium library offers): Higher per-use rates but track locked to one library only.

**Key Question to Ask Any Library:**
1. What is the artist's share per license or subscription distribution?
2. Can I remain with my PRO? (Answer should always be yes — don't sign away PRO rights)
3. Non-exclusive or exclusive? For how long? Any lock-up period?
4. Do you file cue sheets with PROs on my behalf?

Drafting your library submission checklist now.
expected.notes: Sync library payment models — per-license split, subscription blanket, buyout comparison

scenario: Expert: Most-Favored-Nation clause in sync licensing deals
framing: advocate

input.user_message: A music supervisor mentioned they want to include a 'most-favored-nation' clause in my sync license. What does this mean and should I accept it?

expected.output_sample:
Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) clauses are one of the most important and commonly misunderstood terms in sync licensing — and they cut both ways.

**What MFN Means:**
An MFN clause means: 'If any other licensor in this production receives better financial terms than you received for a comparable use, you automatically receive the same improvement.'

Example: You license your song for $5,000. Another artist in the same film licenses for $8,000 for a comparable placement. With an MFN clause, you're automatically entitled to $8,000.

**Why Supervisors Include MFN:**
MFN protects them from disputes where one artist feels they were treated unfairly compared to another. It simplifies negotiation — everyone gets 'the best deal offered.'

**Why It Can Work For You:**
If you're a less established artist in a production with a big-name artist, MFN ensures you're not lowballed compared to them. You benefit from any better deals others negotiate.

**Why It Can Work Against You:**
If you negotiate a strong deal ($15k) and the production later gives a lower-tier artist $5k for a different use, the supervisor can argue that MFN 'equalizes' — though typically MFN only applies to 'comparable' uses, not all uses in the production.

**Negotiating MFN Language:**
1. Define 'comparable': 'MFN applies to tracks licensed for featured use (>30 seconds) in the same production. Does not apply to background, transitional, or incidental use.'
2. Add a floor, not a ceiling: 'MFN ensures minimum parity — it shall not be used to reduce Licensor's agreed fee.'
3. Notification requirement: 'Licensor shall be notified within 30 days of any license in this production that triggers MFN parity.'

Analyzing the proposed MFN language in your contract now.
expected.notes: MFN clause in sync — definition, both-way implications, negotiation language

scenario: Expert: Exclusive library deal analysis — what you give up and what you gain
framing: advocate

input.user_message: A premium sync library is offering me an exclusive deal — they want exclusive rights to my catalog for 3 years with 60/40 splits and an advance of $10,000. Is this worth it?

expected.output_sample:
A $10k advance + 60/40 split exclusive sounds appealing — but you need to pressure-test it before signing.

**The Core Trade-off:**
You're agreeing that for 3 years, THIS library is the only place your catalog can be licensed. If they don't actively pitch it, or if a better opportunity comes along, you're locked out.

**Critical Questions to Demand Answers To:**

1. **Is the advance recoupable?**
The $10k advance is almost certainly recoupable against your future royalties — meaning you won't see another dollar until the library has earned $10k in your name from sync fees. If annual earnings are $3k, you don't see additional income for 3+ years.

2. **What's the library's active sync team size?**
A library that doesn't actively pitch has your catalog sitting idle. Ask: How many music supervisors do you have relationships with? What's the average placement rate for new catalog signings?

3. **Catalog size requirements?**
Exclusive deals often require minimum catalog sizes (50+ tracks). If you have 20 tracks, they may require you to deliver additional recordings.

4. **Termination rights if they underperform?**
Add: 'If the library generates less than $[X] in licensing revenue in any 12-month period after recoupment, Licensor has the right to terminate this agreement with 60 days notice.'

5. **Reversion at term end**
Do tracks revert to you with clear title at end of 3 years? Or do they retain catalog rights for placements made during the term?

**Counter-Structure:**
- Reduce exclusivity scope: 'Exclusive for sync/licensing only; PRO performance royalties remain with Licensor'
- Add performance guarantee: '$15k in licenses or the deal terminates'
- Reduce term: 18 months with renewal option if performance targets met

$10k advance / 3 years / 60-track catalog = $167/track — only attractive if they actively place.
expected.notes: Exclusive library deal — recoupment, performance triggers, reversion, counter-structure

scenario: Expert: Sub-publishing licensing waterfall — how international licensing income flows
framing: advocate

input.user_message: My publisher says they work with sub-publishers in other countries. A sync deal in Germany went through our sub-publisher there. How do I know what percentage I actually receive at the end of all these middlemen?

expected.output_sample:
Sub-publishing waterfalls can take multiple cuts before you see income. Here's how to map what you actually receive:

**The Waterfall — Germany Example:**

Step 1: German production company pays sync license fee to...
Step 2: Your German sub-publisher (collected sync fee) → takes their commission
Step 3: Sub-publisher remits net to your primary US publisher
Step 4: Your US publisher takes their share
Step 5: You receive the remainder

**Typical Commission Rates:**
- German sub-publisher commission: 15–25% of what they collect
- Your US publisher share: depends on your deal (co-pub = they keep publisher share; admin = 10–20%)
- GEMA (German PRO) also collects performance royalties separately and pays the writer share directly to you/your PRO via reciprocal agreement

**Example Math:**
- German sync fee: €10,000
- Sub-publisher takes 20%: €2,000 → you see €8,000 at US publisher level
- US publisher takes their co-pub share (say 25%): €2,000 → you see €6,000
- Effective rate: 60% of original fee

**'At Source' vs. 'At Receipt' — Critical Contract Term:**
- 'At receipt' royalty calculation: Your % calculated AFTER the sub-publisher has already taken their cut. You're not protected from high sub-publisher commissions.
- 'At source' royalty calculation: Your % calculated from the ORIGINAL fee before any sub-publisher deduction. This is dramatically better — insist on 'at source' in your publishing agreement.

**Transparency Protection:**
Your contract should include: 'Publisher shall provide Licensor with full accounting of all sub-publishing arrangements, including sub-publisher commission rates and specific amounts remitted to Publisher, within 90 days of each accounting period.'

Auditing your sub-publishing waterfall now.
expected.notes: Sub-publishing waterfall — at source vs. at receipt, commission stacking, transparency clause

scenario: Expert: Library deal reversion clause negotiation — getting your catalog back
framing: advocate

input.user_message: I signed a music library deal 3 years ago and it just expired. The library says some of my tracks are still 'in active placement discussions' and they might have rights for those. What do I actually own now and can I license these tracks elsewhere?

expected.output_sample:
Post-term reversion is often the most contested part of library deals because of 'active placement discussions' and 'licenses in flight.' Here's how to evaluate your situation:

**Read the Termination/Reversion Clause Carefully:**
Most library deals include one of these post-term structures:

1. **Clean reversion at term end**: All rights return to you, full stop. Any placement negotiations in progress die. This is the most favorable — if your contract says this, you're free.

2. **Tail period for licenses in flight**: The library retains the right to complete and execute any licensing negotiations that were formally underway during the term, for a defined period (typically 6–12 months post-term). 'Formally underway' should mean documented — written pitch to a supervisor, not just 'we were thinking about pitching it.'

3. **Perpetual use for existing placements**: Songs already placed (e.g., in a show that's still airing) continue under the original license terms. This is standard and fair — they licensed the song for a production that's still active. You get the royalties from that placement.

**The Library's Claim — How to Test It:**
1. Request in writing: 'Please provide documentation of all 'active placement discussions' as of the term expiration date, including email correspondence with music supervisors, production company names, and placement fee amounts under discussion.'
2. If they can't provide documentation within 30 days, the claim is likely unfounded.
3. For perpetual use on existing placements: Request a complete list of all executed licenses for your catalog during the term.

**The Clean Break:**
For tracks with NO active placements: Send written notice 'As of [date], this agreement has expired. All rights to the following tracks [list] have reverted to [Your Name/Company]. No further licensing by [Library] is authorized.'

Reviewing your contract reversion language now.
expected.notes: Post-term library reversion — tail period, perpetual use vs. clean reversion, documentation demands

scenario: Expert: Video game licensing — perpetual license and interactive use terms
framing: advocate

input.user_message: A video game company wants to license my track. They want 'perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide rights for interactive media including all current and future game formats.' What does this mean and how do I price it?

expected.output_sample:
Video game licensing requires understanding the specific interactive use rights and the unique longevity of games vs. traditional media.

**Breaking Down 'Perpetual, Irrevocable, Worldwide, Interactive Media':**
- 'Perpetual': Forever. Games are sold and replayed for decades.
- 'Irrevocable': You cannot terminate the license even if you change your mind. Standard in game deals.
- 'Interactive media, all current and future formats': This includes the original game, DLC (downloadable content), expansions, sequels that include this title's soundtrack, streaming via cloud gaming (Xbox Cloud, PlayStation Now), remasters, mobile ports, and potentially esports events.

**What It Does NOT Include (unless explicitly stated):**
- Game trailers and advertisements (require separate trailer sync license)
- Gaming convention/expo public performance (may trigger PRO licensing)
- Licensed merchandise featuring the song

**Pricing Framework for Video Game Sync:**
- Indie game (<$5 budget, <500k units expected): $500–$2,500 per track
- Mid-tier game ($500k–$5M budget): $2,500–$10,000 per track
- AAA title ($50M+ budget): $10,000–$75,000+ per track (sometimes up to $500k for main theme)
- Mobile game with in-app purchase revenue: Add a 'backend royalty' provision — 0.5–1% of revenue over $1M threshold

**Negotiation Points:**
1. 'All future game formats' is broad — limit to game formats existing as of contract date, with first right of refusal for new platforms
2. Exclude trailer use: 'License does not include use in trailers, promotional videos, or advertising materials — these require separate licenses'
3. Streaming gaming: Twitch/YouTube gameplay streaming may generate PRO performance royalties — confirm your PRO rights are preserved
4. DLC expansion: If the game sells DLC that uses this track, request a supplemental fee for each major DLC release

Drafting license with limited 'future formats' scope now.
expected.notes: Video game sync — interactive use scope, perpetual irrevocable terms, pricing tiers, DLC/streaming

scenario: Expert: Trailer sync deal — negotiating above the typical flat fee
framing: advocate

input.user_message: A major film trailer company wants my track. They're offering $5,000 flat. I've heard trailer sync is one of the highest-paying sync markets. Am I being underpaid?

expected.output_sample:
Trailer sync is indeed one of the most lucrative sync categories — and $5,000 for a major studio trailer is likely below market. Here's the context:

**Trailer Sync Market Rates:**
- Indie film theatrical trailer: $2,500–$10,000
- Mid-major film theatrical: $5,000–$25,000
- Major studio theatrical trailer (Disney, Warner, Universal): $15,000–$75,000
- Teaser trailer (30–60 seconds, online only): $5,000–$25,000
- Super Bowl ad/trailer: $50,000–$150,000+

**The $5k offer for a major studio is low.** Counter at $15,000–$25,000 depending on your leverage and their budget tier.

**What the Fee Should Cover (define it explicitly):**
- 'Theatrical trailer use' = playing before films in movie theaters
- 'Online/digital trailer use' = YouTube, social media, Apple/Google trailers
- 'TV spots' = TV advertising for the film — typically a SEPARATE license
- Duration: 90–120 second trailer use
- Territory: Worldwide (standard for major studio)

**Step Deal Structure for Trailers:**
Professional trailer deals are often structured in steps:
- Step 1: $3,000 for use in test trailer / internal review (non-public)
- Step 2: $12,000 additional for public theatrical release (total $15,000)
- Step 3: $8,000 additional for TV broadcast promotion (total $23,000)

This structure lets both parties commit incrementally.

**Your Leverage:**
If the trailer has already been cut with your song, your leverage is at its maximum — they've committed. If they're still in the 'we'd like to use it' phase, you have less leverage but the music hasn't been matched yet.

Analyzing their offer terms and drafting your counter now.
expected.notes: Trailer sync rates — major studio pricing, step deal structure, use scope definition

scenario: Expert: Perpetuity clause negotiation — term limits and reversion strategies
framing: advocate

input.user_message: Almost every sync deal I get offered asks for 'in perpetuity' rights. Is that ever acceptable or should I always push back on this? What are my options?

expected.output_sample:
Whether to accept perpetuity depends entirely on the context. Here's the framework:

**When Perpetuity Is Standard and Acceptable:**
- Film theatrical release: The film may play for 50+ years. Renegotiating the license every 5 years is impractical. Perpetuity + appropriate upfront fee is standard practice.
- Major TV show (Game of Thrones, Stranger Things): Show runs indefinitely, reruns exist forever. Perpetuity is expected.
- Published video game: Can be sold for decades.

In these cases: Accept perpetuity — but ensure the FEE reflects the permanent grant.

**When to Push Back on Perpetuity:**
- Online content with expected short shelf-life (social media campaigns, brand videos): These don't need perpetuity — negotiate a 2–5 year term with options to renew.
- Corporate/training videos: Use life of the project, not perpetuity.
- Any scenario where the licensor is small or the use is limited.

**Alternatives to Perpetuity:**

1. **Fixed term with renewal option**: 'License term: 5 years from release date. Licensor grants Licensee first option to renew for additional 5-year terms at [mutually agreed fee or 2x original fee].'

2. **Exploitation window approach**: 'License covers the theatrical/broadcast window only (years 1–7 from release). Streaming/home video rights continue in perpetuity.' This limits perpetuity to certain media types.

3. **Escalating step-up fees**: Accept perpetuity but require payments at milestones — 'If the production exceeds 50M views/streams worldwide, Licensor receives a supplemental fee of $2,500.'

4. **Reversion if commercially abandoned**: 'If Licensee ceases commercial exploitation of the production for a period exceeding 3 years, Licensor may request reversion of the license.'

**Rule of thumb**: Perpetuity is acceptable when the fee reflects permanent value. Short-term uses at perpetuity pricing = you're leaving money on the table.
expected.notes: Perpetuity clause strategy — when to accept, alternatives, step-up fees, abandonment reversion

scenario: Expert: All-rights licensing clause — identifying and refusing rights grabs
framing: advocate

input.user_message: I was sent a sync contract that says 'Licensor grants all rights, title, and interest in the composition and sound recording, including all copyrights and renewals.' This is just a sync license, right? Why does it mention all rights?

expected.output_sample:
STOP. Do not sign this. This is not a sync license — this is a copyright assignment agreement disguised as a sync deal.

**The Language That Should Alarm You:**
'grants all rights, title, and interest in the composition and sound recording, including all copyrights and renewals'

**Sync License vs. Copyright Assignment:**
- A sync LICENSE grants permission to use the music in a specific way. You remain the owner.
- 'All rights, title, and interest... including all copyrights' is a TRANSFER OF OWNERSHIP. You are selling or giving away the song itself.

This is legally similar to signing over the deed to your house. If you sign this, they own the song.

**How This Differs from Standard Sync Language:**
Legitimate sync license language:
'Licensor grants Licensee a non-exclusive/exclusive license to synchronize the composition and master recording in [specific production] for [term] in [territory].'

The word 'license' means permission to use. 'Grant all rights, title, and interest' means transfer of ownership.

**Response:**
Refuse to sign as written. Respond: 'This language appears to assign copyright ownership rather than grant a license. We are prepared to grant a sync license for this specific production with defined terms, but we are not in a position to assign ownership of the copyright. Please revise with standard license language.'

**Work-for-Hire Red Flag:**
Also watch for: 'This work constitutes a work-for-hire under 17 U.S.C. § 101.' For existing music, this language is largely unenforceable — but it signals a company trying to claim ownership. Reject it.

Reviewing the full contract for additional red flags now.
expected.notes: All-rights copyright assignment disguised as sync license — red flag identification, rejection response

scenario: Expert: Neighboring rights release clause — waiving performing rights in sync deals
framing: advocate

input.user_message: A contract has a clause saying I 'waive all neighboring rights claims' in connection with this sync license. My manager said I should never sign that. Is he right?

expected.output_sample:
Your manager is absolutely right — a neighboring rights waiver in a sync deal is a significant overreach that you should refuse.

**What Neighboring Rights Are:**
Neighboring rights (also called 'related rights' in some territories) are separate from sync rights. They are the performance royalties owed to:
- The master rights owner (you, if you own the recording) when the RECORDING is broadcast on radio, TV, or streaming
- The featured performer (you) as an artist credit on the recording

These are collected by SoundExchange (US), PPL (UK), SOCAN (Canada), etc. — separately from sync license fees.

**Why You Should Refuse to Waive Them:**
A sync license grants the right to use your music in a specific production. Neighboring rights royalties arise from BROADCASTING that production on TV or radio — this is a separate right that you retain even after granting the sync.

If you waive neighboring rights: You lose all backend performance royalties from any broadcast of this production, worldwide, forever.

For a TV show that airs in 50 countries, this could be tens of thousands of dollars in performance royalties you'd never collect.

**The Legitimate Ask vs. Overreach:**
Some sync deals legitimately ask you to waive 'direct licensing claims' against the broadcaster (because broadcasters pay blanket performance licenses to PROs/neighboring rights agencies — individual artists shouldn't be pursuing direct claims separately).

That's different from waiving all neighboring rights. The correct response:
'Licensor agrees not to pursue direct claims against broadcasters in territories where blanket licenses cover this use. Licensor does not waive neighboring rights payments collected on their behalf by SoundExchange, PPL, or any qualifying rights organization.'

This is standard protective language. Any legitimate production company should accept it.
expected.notes: Neighboring rights waiver red flag — what to refuse, what's legitimate, protective contract language

scenario: Expert: Music supervisor outreach strategy — positioning for sync placements
framing: advocate

input.user_message: I want to start getting my music in TV shows and films. I know I need to reach out to music supervisors but I don't know how to approach them professionally. What's the right strategy?

expected.output_sample:
Music supervisor outreach has a specific etiquette that separates artists who get placements from those who get ignored. Here's the professional approach:

**What Music Supervisors Actually Need:**
A music supervisor's job is to find music for specific scenes. They need:
1. Music that fits the brief (mood, tempo, genre, era)
2. Music that's 'clearable' quickly (you own all rights, ready to license fast)
3. A contact who responds quickly and doesn't overcomplicate the deal

**The Pitch Format:**
- Subject: [Artist Name] | [Genre/Mood] | Stems Available
- Body (3–4 sentences max): Who you are, what type of music, 1–2 specific tracks with SoundCloud or private download link, one sentence about clearance ('I own 100% of master and publishing rights and can turn around a license within 24 hours')
- Never attach audio files to a cold email — always link
- Never pitch more than 2–3 tracks in the first email

**'One-Stop Shop' Is Your Biggest Asset:**
If you own both the master and publishing (sync + master license), you're a one-stop shop — the supervisor can clear your music with one email to one person. This is enormously valuable. Always state it explicitly.

**Where to Find Music Supervisors:**
- Music Supervisor Guild (MSG) — professional directory
- IMDb Pro — production companies' credits show their supervisors
- LinkedIn — 'music supervisor [show name]'
- Networking events: SXSW, MIDEM, The Guild Summit

**What Not to Do:**
- Don't follow up more than once after 2 weeks
- Don't send unsolicited tracks without a specific brief or reason
- Don't pitch music you don't own or need complex clearance for

**Better than cold outreach: Sync libraries with supervisor relationships** — let them pitch on your behalf while you build direct relationships over time.

Pulling music supervisor contact strategies for your genre now.
expected.notes: Music supervisor pitch strategy — one-stop shop positioning, pitch format, where to find supervisors

scenario: Expert: Uncleared sample discovered after release — damage control and retroactive clearance
framing: advocate

input.user_message: I just found out my producer used an uncleared sample in a track I released 8 months ago. It's been streaming with 400,000 streams. What do I do now?

expected.output_sample:
This is a real risk situation that requires immediate action. Here's the triage:

**Immediate Risk Assessment:**
400,000 streams × $0.004/stream = ~$1,600 in income from a track with an uncleared sample. The rights holder (if they discover it) can:
- File a DMCA takedown (immediate streaming removal)
- Demand all royalties earned + damages
- In worst case, file copyright infringement litigation

**Step 1: Identify the Sample Owners**
You need to clear BOTH:
1. The master recording rights owner (record label or artist who made the original recording)
2. The publishing/composition rights owner (songwriter and publisher)

For each, find the current rights holder through: ASCAP/BMI (for publishing), label credits on the original track, AllMusic, Discogs.

**Step 2: Retroactive Clearance (Act Before They Find You)**
Approach the rights holders proactively before they file a claim. A proactive clearance approach is significantly less expensive than a demand letter.

Retroactive sample clearance typical outcomes:
- Upfront buyout: $500–$5,000 for smaller samples, $10k–$50k+ for recognizable hooks
- Revenue share: Rights holder receives percentage of all past and future streaming income from the track
- Track removal: They may simply demand the track come down — at which point you re-release an edited version without the sample

**Step 3: Check Your Producer Agreement**
If you hired the producer, your contract should include a warranty that the beat they delivered was 100% original or cleared. If the producer warranted clearance and the sample was theirs to clear, they may be liable for the retroactive clearance cost.

**Step 4: Consider a Re-Record**
If clearance is unaffordable, hire musicians to replay the sampled element and re-release the track. You replace the uncleared master sample with an original recording.

Helping you identify the rights holders now.
expected.notes: Uncleared sample retroactive clearance — DMCA risk, proactive approach, re-record option

scenario: Expert: International sub-publishing deal structure — territory carve-outs
framing: advocate

input.user_message: A European music publisher wants to be my sub-publisher for Europe. My US publisher says I can do this separately. How does sub-publishing territory carve-outs work and what should I negotiate?

expected.output_sample:
A European sub-publishing deal is a territory carve-out from your overall publishing rights — a common and legitimate structure. Here's how to protect yourself:

**Territory Definition (Be Specific):**
Don't accept vague 'Europe' definitions. Define explicitly:
- 'Licensed Territory: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom' — or 'European Union member states as of January 2026 + UK + Norway + Switzerland'
- Explicitly exclude: 'For clarity, USA, Canada, Japan, Australia, and all territories not listed above are excluded.'

**Commission Structure — At Source Is Critical:**
Sub-publisher commission: 15–25% of what they collect.
But HOW that's calculated matters enormously:

- 'At receipt' (unfavorable): US publisher receives 80% of what European sub-publisher collected. Then applies your deal (e.g., 70/30 admin deal) to THAT amount.
  - Example: €1,000 → sub-publisher takes 20% → US publisher receives €800 → you get 70% = €560 (you got 56%)

- 'At source' (favorable): Your percentage is applied to the full €1,000, not after sub-publisher deduction.
  - Example: €1,000 → you get 70% = €700 (you got 70%)

**Non-Performance Reversion:**
Add: 'If sub-publisher fails to collect or register income exceeding €[2,500] within any 12-month period of the term, Licensor has the right to terminate this agreement with 60 days written notice.'

**Term and Renewal:**
- Standard: 3–5 years with notification window (6 months before end) to terminate or renew
- Add: 'Automatic renewal shall not occur without express written consent from Licensor'

**Your US Publisher's Role:**
Most US publishers have existing sub-publishing relationships in Europe already. Confirm with them: Do they have a European sub-publisher already? If yes, this new deal may duplicate or conflict. Clarify the chain before signing.

Drafting the territory-specific sub-publishing framework now.
expected.notes: European sub-publishing carve-out — territory definition, at-source calculation, non-performance reversion

scenario: Expert film/TV deal review

input.user_message: A Netflix documentary has offered a one-time buy-out fee of $3,500 for my track in perpetuity across all platforms, all territories. Walk me through evaluating this against a per-use royalty structure.

expected.output_sample:
A $3,500 buy-out in perpetuity for 'All Media, Known and Unknown, Worldwide' is a standard initial lowball offer from streaming platforms. Here is the strict evaluation logic:

1. THE BUY-OUT DANGER:
A true buy-out means no backend performance royalties when the documentary airs. Netflix avoids paying PROs (ASCAP/BMI) for direct-to-consumer streaming in some territories. $3,500 is your entire compensation forever.

2. THE COUNTER-PROPOSAL:
Reject the total buy-out. Counter with: 'We agree to a $3,500 Sync and Master use fee for SVOD (Streaming Video On Demand) rights worldwide for a term of 5 years. Any theatrical release, linear broadcast (cable/network TV), or physical media requires an additional step-up fee.'

3. CARVING OUT YOUR RIGHTS:
You MUST explicitly carve out 'Soundtrack Rights' and 'Artist's owned DSP streaming rights'. If you don't, the phrasing 'in perpetuity across all platforms' could theoretically give them the ability to claim revenue when the song is streamed on Spotify or placed on an official soundtrack album.

4. THE 'ALL MEDIA' TRAP:
If the documentary is sold to an airline, educational institution, or rebroadcast on traditional linear TV, a per-use structure would generate PRO royalties. A buy-out kills that. If they demand a buy-out, counter at $10,000 to offset the lost lifetime performance revenue.

scenario: Advising on the viral network implications of combining AGPLv3 code with proprietary software via gRPC for both SaaS and on-premise distribution.
framing: A CTO wants to use an AGPLv3 database backend, communicating with a proprietary Go microservice via gRPC. They plan to host this as a SaaS offering and also distribute it as an on-premise enterprise appliance.

input.user_message: We are architecting a system where our proprietary Go application communicates with an unmodified AGPLv3-licensed database purely over gRPC. We will host this as a SaaS, but also ship Docker containers for on-premise enterprise deployments. Does Section 13 of the AGPLv3 trigger a copyleft effect on our Go code in either scenario? How does the 'aggregate' exception apply here?

expected.output_sample: Under the AGPLv3, the copyleft effect is triggered by two mechanisms: traditional distribution (Section 10) and remote network interaction (Section 13). For your SaaS offering, Section 13 applies to the AGPL backend, requiring you to offer the source code of the AGPL component to users interacting with it over a network. However, communicating purely over gRPC at arm's length typically constitutes an 'aggregate' rather than a derivative work, provided the Go app and AGPL database run in separate memory spaces and do not rely on intimate data structures. Therefore, your proprietary Go code is likely shielded from the viral effect in the SaaS model. For the on-premise deployment, shipping the Docker containers constitutes 'conveying' under Section 10. While conveying them together on the same medium creates an aggregate, you must ensure the AGPL component's source is provided or offered. The gRPC boundary remains critical: if the Go code is a separate program, it remains proprietary, but you must strictly adhere to the AGPL's conveying requirements for the database container.

scenario: Clearing global synchronization and master rights for a multi-writer track with an uncleared sample for a global SVOD series.
framing: A music supervisor is trying to clear a hip-hop track for a global Netflix series. The track has 6 credited writers, two different publishers, and contains an uncleared drum sample. They need a buyout but publishers are demanding MFN.

input.user_message: I'm clearing a track for a worldwide SVOD series (all media excluding theatrical). The master is owned by an indie label, but the publishing is split between 6 writers across 2 publishers (Sony and a boutique admin). One publisher insists on a Most Favored Nations (MFN) clause for the sync fee. Furthermore, there's an uncleared drum break sample in the master. How do I structure the quote requests and mitigate the risk of the uncleared sample while honoring the MFN?

expected.output_sample: To navigate this, you must explicitly structure your quote requests to address fractional licensing, MFN, and the sample risk. First, request quotes for the Sync (publishing) and Master Use rights on a 100% basis, stating the proposed fee is 'subject to MFN with all co-publishers and the master owner.' Because of the MFN, whatever the highest fee negotiated by any single publisher or the label becomes the fee for all parties on a pro-rata basis. Second, regarding the uncleared drum sample: you cannot clear the master without the label providing an indemnification against third-party claims.
